items.answer: The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.
Lighting is a stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that assigns color to a constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

Rasterization is the fifth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms continuous device coordinate descriptions into discrete pixel-grid screen descriptions by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.
Object representation is the first stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that defines the objects that form the rendered image in each object's local coordinate system.
A local coordinate system is an object's own coordinate system in the 3D graphics pipeline, in which objects are defined before modeling transformation transforms them to the world coordinate system.

Modeling transformation is the second stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms an object’s local coordinate description into the common world coordinate system so that objects can be assembled into a scene.

questions.question: What is the main reason a VR developer should study computer graphics before tackling rendering?
options: It covers the combination of audio with the visual scene
It covers the transformation of objects into world coordinates
It covers the placement of a display close to the user's eyes
It covers the production of the displayed scene
questions.explanation: Computer graphics is needed because it covers rendering, the process that produces the scene shown on the display. Transforming coordinates, placing a display, or adding audio are not the stated link to understanding rendering.

questions.question: What is the purpose of calling object representation the first stage of the 3D graphics pipeline?
options: to calculate intensities
to determine pixel intensities
to simplify naming
to project the scene
questions.explanation: The first-stage label is a simplification for naming; object representation is not where pixel intensities are calculated or the scene is projected.

data.text: Computer graphics supplies the framework for understanding VR rendering. Rendering is the key immersive process that displays the scene in front of the user's eyes on the display, so its complexities need graphics knowledge. The 3D graphics pipeline then introduces object representation as the first stage for simplicity, with no pixel-intensity computation.
points: Some computer graphics knowledge is needed to understand VR rendering, which renders the scene in front of the user's eyes.
Object representation in the 3D graphics pipeline is called the first stage for simplicity but has no pixel-intensity computation.

questions.question: Which stage of the 3D graphics pipeline takes a scene description from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system?
options: The modeling transformation stage
The lighting stage
The scan conversion stage
The viewing pipeline stage
questions.explanation: The viewing pipeline includes the transformations that take the scene from world coordinates, through view and projection, to device coordinates. Modeling transformation ends at world coordinates, lighting remains in world coordinates, and scan conversion starts from device coordinates.

data.text: The 3D graphics pipeline processes a 3D scene through five stages in a fixed order. It begins with local object representation, then modeling transformation to world coordinates, and lighting in the world coordinate reference frame. The viewing pipeline then converts the scene to device coordinates through viewing transformation, clipping, hidden-surface removal, projection, and window-to-viewport transformation, and scan conversion finally yields screen or pixel-grid coordinates.
points: The 3D graphics pipeline has five ordered stages: object representation, modeling, lighting, viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.

activities.title: Order the stages of the 3D graphics pipeline

items.title: Order the stages of the 3D graphics pipeline
steps: Represent the object in local coordinates
Transform the object into world coordinates
Compute the object's color in world coordinates
Apply viewing transformation, clipping, hidden-surface removal, projection, and viewport mapping
Convert the scene to a pixel grid

questions.question: What is the main purpose of applying a modeling transformation to an object's local description?
options: To compute pixel intensities during a lighting stage
To remove hidden surfaces in a view coordinate system
To place it in a world coordinate system
To estimate the initial pose of a tracked sensor
questions.explanation: Modeling transformation changes an object's local-coordinate description into the world coordinate system so separate objects can be assembled into one scene. Hidden-surface removal, lighting, and pose estimation belong to other parts of the XR or graphics pipeline.

questions.question: What does an object's local coordinate system description specify?
options: The position and dimensions in its own reference frame
The tracker's initial alignment with the physical room
The motion of a receiver attached to a headset
The viewer's position and orientation in the world scene
questions.explanation: A local coordinate system description is the object's individual definition in its own coordinate reference frame. Viewer pose, tracker registration, and receiver motion describe tracked entities, not the object's own coordinate definition.

questions.question: What do combinations of translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing allow in modeling transformation?
options: Converting the scene from device coordinates to screen pixels
Eliminating the need for a world coordinate system
Estimating the pose of a physical tracked object
Creating the transformations required to construct a scene
questions.explanation: Translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing are the basic modeling operations; combined, they can produce the transformations needed to construct a scene. Pose estimation and device-coordinate conversion are separate tracking or pipeline steps.

data.text: Modeling transformation, called stage 2, uses an object’s local coordinate description to place that object in a common world scene. This lets multiple objects be assembled as a scene. Its basic transformations—translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing—combine to form any transformation required for the scene.
points: Modeling transformation, stage 2, places an object described in its own coordinate frame in a common world scene.
The basic transformations are translation, rotation around an axis, scaling, and shearing; combinations create any needed scene transformation.

questions.question: Why is a two-dimensional transformation represented by a 3 by 3 matrix in homogeneous coordinates?
options: because a scan-conversion coordinate is added
because one extra dimension is added
because a viewing coordinate is added
because a clipping coordinate is added
questions.explanation: A homogeneous-coordinate representation adds one dimension to the original coordinates, so a 2D transformation needs a 3 by 3 matrix. Pipeline stages such as viewing, clipping, or scan conversion do not account for this added matrix dimension.

questions.question: Which set of parameters is used for the standard 2D transformations in homogeneous coordinates?
options: translation amounts, an axis, clipping bounds, and projection factors
rotation angle, light intensities, scan lines, and pixel factors
scaling factors, a depth value, viewport edges, and window factors
translation amounts, an angle, scaling factors, and shearing factors
questions.explanation: The 2D homogeneous-coordinate matrices use translation amounts, a rotation angle, scaling factors, and shearing factors. Axes, clipping, projection, lighting, and viewport quantities belong to other pipeline stages, not to the basic 2D transformation parameters.

questions.question: How is a point on an object transformed from its local coordinate system to the world coordinate system?
options: by adding the point's coordinates to the translation amounts in the composite matrix
by representing the point as a row vector and multiplying it by the viewing matrix
by representing the point as a column vector and multiplying it by the transformation matrix
by projecting the point from view coordinates onto the viewport matrix
questions.explanation: A local point is written as a column vector and multiplied by the transformation matrix to obtain its corresponding world-coordinate point. A row-vector form with a viewing matrix points to the viewing stage, and projection or coordinate addition is not the local-to-world transformation step.

data.text: Homogeneous coordinates give transformations a matrix form, so 2D operations such as translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing can be expressed with 3x3 matrices, while 3D transformations can use 4x4 matrices. Once a point is a column vector, multiplying it by the transformation matrix converts local coordinates to world coordinates, ideally.
points: Transformations are typically represented by homogeneous-coordinate matrices: 2D can use 3x3 for translation, rotation, scaling, shearing, while 3D uses 4x4.
A local point (x, y) is represented as column vector P and multiplied by S, ideally giving a world point.

questions.question: When is a composite transformation matrix used while placing an object in a world coordinate scene?
options: When a viewing transformation is required for the camera
When color computation is required for the surface
When several basic transformations are required for the object
When any modeling transformation is required for the object
questions.explanation: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic transformations on an object. A single modeling transformation, a camera viewing transformation, or color assignment does not by itself require a composite matrix.

questions.question: How is a composite transformation matrix formed from the matrices of the transformations that are applied?
options: By placing the first applied matrix leftmost and the later matrices to its right
By placing the matrices in any order before multiplying them
By placing the last applied matrix rightmost and the earlier matrices to its left
By placing the first applied matrix rightmost and the later matrices to its left
questions.explanation: The matrices are arranged right to left according to the order of application: the transformation applied first is placed rightmost, and later transformations are placed to its left. For example, if scaling is applied first and translation second, the translation matrix is to the left of the scaling matrix.

questions.question: If M is the composite transformation matrix and A is a current vertex, how is the transformed vertex A′ calculated?
options: M is multiplied with A
M is added to A
A is multiplied with M
A is added to M
questions.explanation: Each current vertex is multiplied by the composite transformation matrix to obtain the transformed vertex, as in A′ = M A. Reversing the multiplication order or using addition does not follow the stated vertex transformation.

questions.question: Why does the rectangle-to-chimney example need a composite matrix rather than one basic transformation?
options: Because it must be translated once and then rotated about an axis
Because it must be sheared in one direction and then translated to its final position
Because it must be scaled in one direction and then translated to its final position
Because it must be rotated about an axis and then scaled in one direction
questions.explanation: The rectangle cannot become the chimney-like shape with one basic transformation: it must be halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and then moved so that its origin vertex reaches the final position. Using the wrong sequence of these transformations could produce an incorrect transformed result because matrix multiplication is not commutative.

data.text: A composite transformation matrix combines several basic transformations when a world-coordinate scene cannot be built with only one. The rectangle-to-chimney example supplies the needed scale and translation values, and those matrices are multiplied in the right-to-left application order required by noncommutative matrix multiplication. Applying the resulting matrix to each current vertex gives the transformed vertices.
points: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world-coordinate scene needs multiple basic transformations.
The rectangle-to-chimney worked example needs scale factors Sx 0.5, Sy 1, and translation Tx 5, Ty 5.
In the example, translation is placed left of scaling, because matrices are ordered by application right-to-left and multiplication is noncommutative.
To obtain world-coordinate vertices, multiply each current vertex by the composite transformation matrix.

questions.question: Why can a lack of color assignment reduce the quality of a rendered scene?
options: Because the display cannot show a virtual environment without colors
Because shading models become unavailable without a lighting model
Because the scene loses its geometry when colors are missing
Because properly assigned colors support the perception of depth
questions.explanation: Properly assigned colors help the viewer perceive depth, and failing to assign colors reduces the quality of experience. Shading models may rely on lighting models, but that dependency is not the reason missing colors harm perceived depth.

questions.question: How are shading models related to lighting models in computer graphics?
options: They follow lighting models after colors have been assigned to objects
They approximate lighting models to reduce computation
They replace lighting models by removing color assignment entirely
They replicate lighting models exactly to increase computation
questions.explanation: Shading models are approximations of lighting-model color assignment and rely on lighting models; their role is to lower computational cost while preserving experience quality. They are not exact replacements, and they are not used only after colors are assigned.

questions.question: What do lighting models typically compute before the color values are mapped for a display?
options: Unbounded real numbers, usually normalized between 0 and 1
Fixed palette entries, usually normalized between 0 and 1
Continuous real numbers, usually normalized between 0 and 1
Discrete display values, usually normalized between 0 and 1
questions.explanation: Lighting models compute color as continuous intensity values, essentially real numbers typically normalized to the range 0 to 1. These continuous values are then mapped to discrete computer-supported values for display.

data.text: Color computation occupies the third stage of the computer graphics pipeline, where objects are given colors so that depth can be perceived. Lighting and shading models are then distinguished by computation: lighting models are more expensive, while shading models approximate them to reduce computation without compromising quality. Lighting models represent colors as continuous intensity values, typically normalized real numbers from 0 to 1, and those values are mapped to discrete values.
points: The third graphics pipeline stage, color computation, uses lighting or shading models to assign colors for depth perception.
Lighting models use more computation, while shading models are approximations that reduce it without compromising experience.
Lighting models compute colors as continuous, typically normalized intensity values from 0 to 1, mapped to discrete values.

questions.question: What determines the color perceived at a point on a surface?
options: The intensity of reflected light reaching the viewer's eye
The intensity of incident light falling on that particular surface point
The intensity of light emitted by the light source
The intensity of light absorbed at that point
questions.explanation: The perceived color is determined by the light actually reflected from the surface point into the viewer's eye. Incident, emitted, or absorbed light does not by itself set the perceived color.

questions.question: Which description matches the ambient light component in the simple lighting model?
options: It is light emitted by the surface point itself
It comes directly from a light source to that particular surface point in the scene
It is produced by specular reflection at a shiny surface
It falls on a surface after reflection from surrounding surfaces
questions.explanation: Ambient light in the simple model is the indirect light that has been reflected by surrounding surfaces before reaching the surface. Direct source light is modeled separately as diffuse or specular reflection.

questions.question: In the simple lighting model, what is the total intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point modeled as?
options: The difference between direct and ambient light intensities
The product of ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities
The maximum of ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities
The sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities
questions.explanation: The simple lighting model adds the ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities to get the total intensity reaching the viewer. Multiplying, taking a maximum, or subtracting would not represent the model's sum.

data.text: A light source emits light that reaches a surface point directly or after surrounding-surface reflection; the incident light reflects to the viewer, and its intensity determines perceived color. A computer graphics lighting model simulates this surface-point reflection to compute the reflected intensity. The simple lighting model expresses that intensity as ambient, diffuse, and specular terms, where ambient is surrounding-surface reflected light, diffuse is direct light reflected diffusely, and specular is direct light reflected specularly as a shiny bright spot.
points: A computer graphics lighting model simulates incident light reflecting at a surface point to compute reflected intensity, the perceived color.
In the simple lighting model, reflected intensity is the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities.
The simple lighting model's ambient component is light reflected from surrounding surfaces onto the surface point.
The simple lighting model's diffuse component is direct light from a light source reflected diffusely from the surface.
The simple lighting model's specular component is direct light from a light source reflected specularly, making a shiny bright spot.

questions.question: What is the ambient component of the reflected light intensity equal to?
options: the ambient light intensity times the specular reflection coefficient
the ambient light intensity times the ambient reflection coefficient
the source light intensity times the ambient reflection coefficient
the ambient light intensity times the diffuse reflection coefficient
questions.explanation: The ambient component is the ambient light intensity at the surface point multiplied by the ambient reflection coefficient. Using source light intensity or the diffuse or specular coefficient would not compute the ambient term.

questions.question: Under what condition does the direct-light diffuse reflection term contribute zero?
options: N dot L is not greater than 0
Ks is not greater than 0
Ka is not greater than 0
V dot r is not greater than 0
questions.explanation: The diffuse term uses the product of Kd, the source intensity, and N dot L only when N dot L is positive; otherwise it is set to zero. The V dot r condition controls the specular term, while Ka and Ks do not determine whether the diffuse term is zero.

questions.question: In the specular component, which quantity is raised to the power Ns?
options: L dot N
V dot r
Ka
N dot L
questions.explanation: The specular component multiplies Ks and the source light intensity by the dot product of the viewer direction and the ideal reflection direction, then raises that dot product to the power Ns. N dot L belongs to the diffuse calculation.

questions.question: Which formula gives the ideal specular reflection direction vector r?
options: twice L dot N times N minus L
twice L dot N times V minus L
twice V dot N times N minus L
twice L dot V times V minus L
questions.explanation: The ideal reflection direction is computed from the light direction and the surface normal as 2(L dot N)N - L. Substituting the viewer direction or using V in place of N changes the result.

data.text: Reflected light is treated as a fraction of incident light, controlled by surface reflection coefficients. The simple lighting model separates reflection into ambient, diffuse, and specular parts, each using its own coefficient. Ambient reflection is a direct coefficient multiplication, while diffuse reflection uses the surface normal and light direction, counting only positive alignment. Phong specular reflection then uses the viewer direction and an ideal reflected direction, computed from the light direction and normal, raised to a power.
points: A surface's reflection coefficient sets the reflected fraction of incident light reaching the viewer.
The simple lighting model uses Ka, Kd, and Ks, each 0.0–1.0, for ambient, diffuse, and specular reflection.
The ambient component is the ambient light intensity multiplied by the ambient reflection coefficient Ka.
Diffuse light is Kd times Is times N dot L, and is zero when N dot L is not positive.
Phong specular uses cos φ = V dot r: Ks Is (V dot r)^Ns, zero if nonpositive, with r = 2(L dot N)N - L.

questions.question: Which phrase best describes the role of radial intensity attenuation in a lighting model?
options: an angular-based cutoff of light intensity
an ambient-based constant of light intensity
a distance-based reduction of intensity
a specular-based increase of light intensity
questions.explanation: Radial attenuation accounts for light becoming weaker as the distance from the source to the surface point increases. Angular cutoff, specular highlighting, and ambient constant brightness describe other lighting effects, not the distance fall-off modeled by radial attenuation.

questions.question: Which effect is angular intensity attenuation primarily used to produce?
options: a specular-like highlight variation with angle
a spotlight-like variation with angle
an ambient-like brightness variation with angle
a diffuse-like shading variation with angle
questions.explanation: Angular intensity attenuation is used mainly for spotlight effects, making points inside the spotlight cone brighter and points outside it darker. Specular, ambient, and diffuse variations are separate parts of the lighting model.

questions.question: In the modified simple lighting model, which term is left unchanged by the radial and angular attenuation factors?
options: the I_D diffuse reflection term
the I_SPEC specular reflection term
the I_D plus I_SPEC reflection term
the I_M intensity term
questions.explanation: The modified model leaves the I_M intensity component unchanged and multiplies the diffuse and specular reflection terms by the radial and angular attenuation factors.

data.text: Lighting in this course extends the simple lighting model with distance and angle dependent weakening of light. Radial attenuation represents the expected fall-off as the surface point moves farther from the light, while angular attenuation controls the bright and dark regions of a spotlight cone. The ambient term stays fixed, and the diffuse and specular terms are scaled by these attenuation factors, so the modified model reduces to the original simple model when both factors equal one.
points: Radial intensity attenuation is often an inverse quadratic function with coefficients a0, a1, and a2 for light fading with distance.
Angular intensity attenuation gives spotlight effects: zero outside angular limit theta and cos(phi)^A1 inside, with A1 adjustable.
In the modified simple lighting model, I_M is unchanged and I_D plus I_SPEC is multiplied by both attenuation factors.
If both attenuation factors are 1, the modified simple lighting model reduces to I_M plus I_D plus I_SPEC.

questions.question: In a colored light source model, how is the emitted light intensity of a source represented?
options: as a three-element cyan, magenta, and yellow vector
as a two-element hue and saturation vector
as a three-element red, green, and blue vector
as a single-component total-intensity vector
questions.explanation: A colored source stores its intensity as separate red, green, and blue components, so its intensity is an RGB vector rather than a single value or another color-space vector.

questions.question: In a colored light source model, what gives the perception of a color in the source's emitted intensity?
options: the combination of its ambient, diffuse, and specular component values
the combination of its red, green, and blue component values
the combination of its radial and angular attenuation factor values
the combination of its minimum and maximum device level values
questions.explanation: The source's emitted color is perceived from the combination of its red, green, and blue intensity components, not from reflection or attenuation terms.

questions.question: For n light sources, how is the illumination at a surface point calculated in the revised lighting model?
options: as ambient light plus the product of contributions from each source
as ambient light plus the average of contributions from each source
as ambient light plus separate contributions from each source
as ambient light plus the maximum of contributions from each source
questions.explanation: With multiple lights, the model adds the ambient term to the independently calculated contribution of every light source. Product, average, or maximum would not represent the summation over sources.

data.text: The lighting model is extended from one intensity value to color and to multiple lights. A colored light source has red, green, and blue intensity components that combine to produce perceived color, and the reflection coefficients are similarly RGB vectors. When n light sources are present, I_P adds ambient light to each source's separately computed contribution, with colored contributions computed for each RGB component.
points: A colored light source's intensity is an RGB vector whose components are computed separately to yield any perceived color.
Reflection coefficients k, kd, and ks are three-element RGB vectors with a value of one in each component.
For n light sources, the lighting model's I_P adds ambient light to each source's contribution, computed separately for RGB.

questions.question: What mismatch requires mapping a lighting-model intensity to a display value?
options: limited frame-buffer entries and unlimited display levels
continuous computed intensities and finite display levels
finite computed intensities and continuous display levels
absolute lighting-model values and relative display levels
questions.explanation: A lighting model can produce an intensity anywhere in a continuous range, while a display can show only a finite set of intensity values, so the computed value must be mapped to a supported display value.

questions.question: Why are successive device-supported intensity levels generated with a multiplicative factor?
options: the photometer records fixed brightness changes between intensity values
the human visual system responds to relative changes between intensity values
the display hardware adds fixed voltage changes between intensity values
the human visual system responds to absolute changes between intensity values
questions.explanation: Successive intensity levels are scaled by a multiplicative factor because perception is based on relative changes between intensities, not on equal absolute changes.

questions.question: How is a lighting-model pixel intensity turned into the pixel's frame-buffer entry?
options: by averaging the two nearest table intensities and storing its bit pattern
by inserting the computed intensity into the frame buffer and storing its bit pattern
by taking the nearest stored table intensity and storing its bit pattern
by selecting the first table intensity above the computed value and storing its bit pattern
questions.explanation: The computed intensity is matched to the nearest intensity stored in the mapping table, and the bit pattern assigned to that table entry is written into the frame buffer.

data.text: A lighting model’s continuous pixel intensity must be converted into the finite intensities that a display can show. The finite levels are computed from the level count, minimum intensity, and maximum 1 as successive r multiples, because humans perceive relative changes between intensity values rather than absolute intensity changes. A table of these levels and bit patterns then lets each computed intensity choose the nearest level for the frame buffer.
points: A lighting model can compute pixel intensities over a continuous 0-to-1 range, while a display supports only finite intensity values.
Successive device-supported intensity levels are I0, rI0, ..., r^nI0, using level count n, minimum I0, and maximum 1.
The multiplicative factor r reflects that humans perceive relative changes between intensity values, not absolute intensity changes.
A table maps a lighting-model pixel intensity to the nearest device-supported intensity, storing its bit pattern in the frame buffer.

questions.question: Why does the order of matrices in a composite transformation matrix affect the transformed result?
questions.reference_answer: A world coordinate scene may require several basic transformations, so their matrices are combined into one composite matrix. The first transformation applied is placed rightmost, and later transformations are placed to its left, so the product applies the operations in the intended order. Because matrix multiplication is not commutative, an incorrect order can produce a wrong transformed result.

questions.question: Why are radial and angular intensity attenuation factors applied to the diffuse and specular components in the modified simple lighting model?
questions.reference_answer: Radial and angular intensity attenuation are needed because light from a source typically diminishes with distance, and angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for spotlight effects. The radial factor, typically an inverse quadratic distance function, accounts for that diminishing. The angular factor is 0 outside the angular limit and varies as the cosine of phi raised to the angular attenuation exponent inside. The modified model multiplies the diffuse and specular sum by these factors, leaving the I_M component unchanged.

questions.question: Why can a shading model be used instead of a lighting model when color is assigned in the computer graphics pipeline?
questions.reference_answer: A shading model is an approximation of the color-assignment methods used by a lighting model, and it relies on that lighting model. It can be used to reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience. This still allows colors to be assigned, which helps depth be perceived and can give a more realistic perception.

questions.question: How does intensity mapping use a multiplicative factor to convert a lighting-model pixel intensity into the value stored in the frame buffer?
questions.reference_answer: A lighting model produces a continuous pixel intensity, while a display supports only finite device-supported values. Because humans perceive relative changes rather than absolute changes, successive device-supported values are powers of a factor times the minimum intensity. A table maps each such value to a bit pattern, and the pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table value for the frame buffer.
